title: The First Moon Spaceport Is Coming. But First We’ll Need Moon Traffic Control - Nautilus
gist: Researchers from Texas A&M, NASA Johnson, and Purdue have proposed 'rules of the road' for lunar orbital traffic ahead of NASA's planned first moon spaceport, warning that poor traffic control could strand spacecraft without enough fuel to return.

insights.claim: NASA aims to open the moon's first spaceport in roughly 20 years, which would require a highly precise lunar air-traffic-control system.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Signals a long-horizon cislunar infrastructure buildout that spawns demand for space-traffic-management capabilities.
insights.locator: in 20 years, NASA will open the moon’s first spaceport

insights.claim: Researchers from Texas A&M University, NASA Johnson Space Center, and Purdue University detailed 'rules of the road' for multiple spacecraft to share the Near Rectilinear Halo Orbit used to dock with the Gateway spaceport.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Early codification of lunar traffic rules foreshadows a new regulatory and engineering domain for space operators.
insights.locator: the researchers lay out “rules of the road”

insights.claim: The NRHO docking path passes within 1,000 miles of the moon's north pole before swinging some 40,000 miles from its south pole, and multiple spacecraft could fly it simultaneously.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Defines the specific orbital geometry that any lunar traffic-management system must coordinate.
insights.locator: will pass within 1,000 miles of the moon’s north pole

insights.claim: Poorly managed lunar air traffic risks sending spacecraft badly off course without the rocket fuel needed to get back.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Frames the high-stakes failure mode that motivates investment in precise lunar navigation.
insights.locator: we risk spacecraft being sent way off course
